title: How a B2B SaaS company should write an about page
metaTitle: How a B2B SaaS company writes about
excerpt: The about page should name who does the work and why that matters to a demo. Skip the origin story unless it changes the buying decision.
alt: A hand holding a stylus over a tablet covered in wireframe sketches, with a keyboard and mouse beside it. The article is about deciding which sentences belong on an about page.
caption: An about page is a set of choices, closer to a working sketch than to a memoir. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is an about page for on a B2B SaaS site?
faqs.answer: It proves that people stand behind the offer. Name who does the work, in roles a buyer will meet on a demo, and name one practice that buyer can test. A manifesto with no names leaves the trust question open.

faqs.question: When should a company include its origin story?
faqs.answer: Include a short origin only when it explains a constraint the product still respects. A story that only explains how the founders met does not change the decision to book a demo. Put any story after the names and the practice, and cut it if it fails that test.

faqs.question: What should an about page leave out?
faqs.answer: Leave hobbies, abstract values, and claims about revenue or headcount you would not repeat on a call. Leave quotes you cannot stand behind. The page is a public promise, so every sentence should survive being forwarded.

markdown:
A B2B SaaS company about page is proof that people stand behind the offer. An operator who already runs software wants to know who does the work and why that should matter to the demo they are about to book. A timeline of the founder's twenties does not answer either question.

Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to book. A garage, a frustration, a late night. Those scenes are easy to write and hard to use. Keep a scene only when it explains a constraint the product still respects. Otherwise the page should spend its words on the people, the judgment, and the kind of buyer they are built for.

## Proof of people, not a memoir

The operator has usually seen the product and the price before they open this page. They are checking for a handoff risk. If we buy this, is there a person who understands the job, or a logo with a chatbot behind it?

Answer that check in the first two paragraphs. Name the work the company does. Name the kind of people who do it. Say how a buyer reaches a human. You do not need a headcount. You need roles that match the offer. Who builds the product. Who sits on the demo. Who answers when the workflow breaks.

Google's guidance on helpful, people-first content treats the question of who is behind a page as part of trust. The about page is where that question is allowed to be the whole point. Write it so a stranger can say who they would be talking to. A manifesto with no names leaves the question open, and an open question at this stage delays the demo.

Keep the tone level. This buyer has read a hundred origin stories. They are not unkind. They are busy. Specific roles will do more than superlatives. "The people who configure approvals sit on the onboarding calls" is proof. "We are passionate operators" is a costume.

## Name who does the work

Use real roles and real responsibilities. A founder who still does demos can say so. An engineer who owns the billing workflow can say so. A support lead who has a name and a domain can say so. If a role is shared, describe the share. "Two people cover implementation, and the same people support the first month."

Photographs help when they are of those people in the work, not a stock table. A portrait with a name and a sentence is enough. The sentence should say what they are accountable for, not a hobby. Hobbies are pleasant. They do not help an operator decide.

If you are early and the team is small, say the truth in plain size. A small team that names its limits is easier to trust than a page of silhouettes implying a department. The operator is buying the product and the attention around it. Attention is more believable when the names are few and specific.

Skip titles that were invented for the page. "Chief vision officer" with no description of the work is a costume again. Use the words the buyer will hear on the call. If the founder leads the demo and writes the spec, say that.

Where someone outside the company does part of the work, say that too. A named security partner. A studio that designed the interface. Invented scale is a short-term comfort and a long-term correction on the first call. The call is a bad place to revise the about page.

## Why this buyer should care

The second job of the page is relevance. Not "we care about customers." Every page says that. Relevance is a reason this operator, with software already in place, should believe these people understand the job.

Write the reason as a practice. You have spent your time on approval chains, or on the month-end close, or on support queues with a backlog. You refuse a certain kind of customization because it breaks the record. You sit with the admin, not only with the executive sponsor. Pick the practices that are true and that change the demo.

One practice, told in four sentences, beats a list of values. Values can stay if they are operational. "We answer the person who does the work, not only the person who signed" is a value an operator can test. "Integrity" is not, because nobody offers the opposite.

Connect the practice to the product screen they already saw. If the homepage shows an approval queue, the about page can say who watches that queue fail in real accounts and what they change because of it. The two pages should feel like one company. The about page is not a separate brand exercise.

Leave industry awards and headcount claims off unless you can show them without stretching. This buyer is allergic to borrowed glory. A single specific practice will outlast a row of badges.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin story earns a place when it explains a constraint the buyer will feel. You built the product because a finance team kept a side spreadsheet, and you still refuse features that recreate the spreadsheet. That story changes the demo. It tells the operator what you will not bend.

A story that only explains how the founders met does not change the demo. It can live in a talk or a dinner. On the page it pushes the names and the practice down, which is the part the operator opened the page to find.

If you keep a story, keep it short and put it after the proof. First who does the work. Then why this buyer should care. Then, if it still helps, the scene that produced the constraint. End the scene by returning to the present product. A story that never comes back to the job is a memoir excerpt.

Read it back and ask one question. Would this paragraph change whether I book the demo, or how I prepare for it? If the answer is no, cut the paragraph. The page will get calmer, and the remaining sentences will get stronger.

## What to leave out of the biography

Leave the childhood. Leave the gap year. Leave a quote about changing the world. Leave a carousel of office dogs unless the dogs are the product, which they are not.

Leave the customer quote you cannot stand behind, and leave any number about revenue, growth, or team size that you would not say on a call with a skeptical finance lead. The about page is a public promise. Treat every sentence as one you will repeat live.

Leave a long list of tools in the stack as a personality. A line can mention the craft if it matters to the buyer. You care about a record that can be audited. You care that an admin can undo a mistake. Those are reasons. A logo garden of databases is not a reason for this audience. They have their own.

Leave the hard sell at the bottom of a personal essay. The action can be present. It should feel like the obvious next step after trust, not like the essay was bait.

## How the page supports the demo

Close with the demo, and say what the about page just changed about that call. They now know who will be in the room, or who will follow up. They know which practice to ask about. Invite them to book with that in hand.

Suggest one question they might bring. "Ask us what we refuse to customize." A page that offers a hard question is more convincing than a page that offers a compliment. The operator has hard questions already. You are showing you have heard them.

Keep a second path for the person who is not ready to book. A link to a proof page, where a constraint and a decision are shown in the product. The about page names the people. It is a thin proof by itself. The thicker proof is the work.

Do not make them hunt for a human. If a direct name is appropriate, give a role-based address or the booking link, and say the response they should expect in ordinary language. "You will get a time, not a drip sequence." That sentence belongs to this page because this page is about people.

## A structure you can publish

Assemble the page in this order.

1. Two sentences on the work and the buyer it is for.
2. Who does the work, with roles tied to the demo and the first month.
3. One practice that this operator can test.
4. The constraint you still respect, with a short origin only if it explains that constraint.
5. What you will not claim.
6. Book a demo, plus the question they should bring.

Then read the page as if you were forwarding it to your own boss. Could they tell who they will meet? Could they tell why these people fit the job? If either answer is shaky, add a fact or cut a flourish. Do not add another paragraph of warmth to cover a missing name.

The about page gets the buyer to the door. The next piece they need is a record of a decision, with the product on screen, so the people you named have something to stand on. Read [what a proof page has to show this buyer](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-b2b-saas-company) before you add another biography.

When the people and the offer should read as one system, from the first screen through the page that names the team, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The work is the pages, in an order a buyer can follow.
